label: KVP-2400 manufactured 16Q1 (22 units): ground_fault x4, grid_ride_through x1, hard_fault x1, cooling_airflow_low x1
headline: The KVP-2400 16Q1 'cohort' is noise, seven unrelated failures across 22 units, and the ground faults inside it are the same combiner-level conductor damage seen on other models at other sites, so no warranty or campaign action is warranted.
action: Close this cohort as ordinary variation and instead track DC ground faults by combiner block across all sites, since CB-level chafing/pinch findings recur at Dry Creek Junction, Sablewood Ridge and Two Rivers Crossing regardless of inverter model or build quarter.
reasoning: The seven events split across four unrelated mechanisms with no shared component: a self-clearing ride-through (WO-2024-00152), a seized cooling fan (WO-2025-00646), a DC contactor swap (WO-2025-00325) and four ground faults (WO-2025-00157, WO-2025-00668, WO-2025-00669, WO-2026-00044), and no asset shows a repeat of the same failure. Against a peer-median expectation of ~3.1 events for 22 units, 7 observed is roughly a one-in-twenty Poisson tail before any correction for the twenty-odd model x quarter cells in this installed base, so it does not survive multiple comparisons. The controls settle it: WO-2026-00631 (Sablewood Ridge) and WO-2026-00205 (Two Rivers Crossing) are near-verbatim chafed-home-run and pinched-connector DC ground faults on non-16Q1 assets at other sites, i.e. the same BOS mechanism that drives the cohort's ground faults is present fleet-wide, which defeats both the cohort story and H1's site-specific workmanship story. H3 is falsified directly by the control asset IDs (KVP24-1618B-0361, KVP24-2136C-0086, KVP24-1643D-0303, KVP24-2419B-0345) whose four-digit segments cannot be build months, so that segment is a lot/line code and there is no evidence of mfg_quarter mis-mapping. H4 fails because the one record with a firmware note, WO-2026-00044 at rev 4.3.0, had a genuine physical finding, while the control at rev 5.0.4 (WO-2026-00205) had one too, so firmware does not separate nuisance from real trips.
contradicting: All four ground faults in the cohort fall at one site (Dry Creek Junction) and two of them resolved to physical DC damage at combiner blocks CB-B01-07 and CB-B01-20 (WO-2025-00668, WO-2026-00044), which is a genuine, if unremarkable, BOS pattern worth tracking at block level rather than by inverter serial. The two NFF/reset ground faults (WO-2025-00157, WO-2025-00669) also consumed parts and 4.8/2.5 labor hours despite 'nothing found', so some real fault or threshold issue may be under-diagnosed; a larger corpus of Dry Creek Junction ground faults across all models could still support H1.

population_detail.description: No defect population established for KVP-2400 16Q1; the ground-fault mechanism observed is fleet-wide BOS conductor damage, not confined to this cohort.

hypotheses.statement: The apparent cohort signal is a site effect: DC-side balance-of-system workmanship (chafed home runs, pinched connectors in combiner boxes) at Dry Creek Junction is generating ground-fault work orders, independent of inverter model or manufacturing quarter.
predictions: 5 of 7 members already sit at Dry Creek Junction; non-KVP-2400 models and other mfg quarters at that same site should show a comparably elevated ground_fault rate per unit.
KVP-2400 16Q1 units at sites other than Dry Creek Junction and Tallow Branch should show a ground_fault rate at or below the peer median of 0.143.

Ground-fault work orders at these sites should keep resolving to component='conductor_or_connector' with combiner/CB-level location references (e.g. CB-B01-07, CB-B01-20) rather than to inverter-internal parts.
Repeat ground faults should cluster by combiner block / string ID rather than by inverter serial.
discriminating_evidence: Cross-tab ground_fault rate by site x model: if site explains the lift and model does not, H1 over a manufacturing-cohort defect.
Presence of DC ground faults on other manufacturers' inverters at Dry Creek Junction.
If the two chafing/pinch findings map to the same combiner block or the same original installation crew, workmanship is confirmed.

hypotheses.statement: This is ordinary variation: 7 events across 22 units over 13 peer-quarters is only ~3-4 events above the peer-median expectation, and the four unrelated symptom types (ground fault, ride-through, contactor, fan) share no component or failure mechanism.
predictions: A Poisson test against expected count (22 x 0.143 ~ 3.1) should not survive multiple-comparison correction across all model x quarter cells examined.

No single component dominates: the cohort's component field should stay spread across central_inverter, dc_contactor, cooling_fan, conductor_or_connector with no repeat failures of the same part on the same asset.
Recurrence flags should remain false and no asset should appear twice in the cohort.
Ranking all model x quarter cohorts by lift should show several other cohorts at similar lift with equally heterogeneous symptom mixes.
discriminating_evidence: Re-run the lift calculation with a per-cohort exposure-adjusted (unit-years online) denominator; if lift collapses toward 1.0, H2.
If ground_fault alone is tested (4 events) rather than all symptoms pooled, does the cohort still separate from peers?
Trend over time: a real defect should show rising or age-correlated event density, ordinary variation should be flat/random across 2024-2026.

hypotheses.statement: The cohort key itself is wrong: asset IDs in the member list encode build months 1601 through 1610, so units built in Q2-Q4 2016 have been mis-assigned to the '16Q1' manufacturing quarter, and the cluster is an artifact of a bad mfg_quarter mapping.
predictions: Parsing the 4-digit segment of asset_id (1601, 1602, 1603, 1607, 1608, 1610) against the mfg_quarter field should show disagreement for the majority of the 22 cohort members.
The 22-unit 'cohort' should turn out to span most or all of calendar 2016, i.e. it is really a model-year population, which mechanically inflates event count relative to a true quarterly lot.
Other 'quarter' cohorts for KVP-2400 should have anomalous or empty membership counts if serials were bucketed by the same faulty rule.

Resolution-code/action disagreements in the same records (NO-FAULT-FOUND with string connectors consumed; ADJUSTED with a DC contactor replaced) indicate the extraction layer is unreliable for cohort-forming fields generally.
discriminating_evidence: Join asset serials to the procurement/commissioning table for true build dates; if build dates span >1 quarter, the cohort dissolves.
Recompute rate using only assets with a verified 16Q1 build date and compare to peer median.
Audit resolution_code vs parts_used consistency across the whole corpus to size the labelling-noise floor.

hypotheses.statement: A subset of the ground faults are nuisance trips from over-sensitive GFDI thresholds on a specific inverter firmware revision (4.3.0 was noted in service), not real insulation faults, so the cohort mixes false alarms with a small number of genuine BOS faults.
predictions: Ground-fault work orders should split cleanly: those resolving to NO-FAULT-FOUND/RESET with clean megger readings (WO-2025-00157, WO-2025-00668/669-type) versus those with a physical finding.
The NFF/reset ground faults should concentrate on assets sharing one firmware revision; assets on other revisions should show only physical-finding ground faults.
NFF ground faults should show short labor hours and near-zero parts consumption, and should recur on the same asset over time if the threshold is never changed.
Reported lost MWh per NFF event should be low relative to hard_fault/contactor events despite similar WO counts.
discriminating_evidence: Extract firmware revision for all 22 cohort assets and cross-tab against NFF-ground-fault count; a clean split confirms H4 and separates it from H1's physical-damage story.
Check whether any asset shows a firmware update followed by cessation of ground-fault WOs.
If megger/insulation-resistance values are recorded, genuine faults show degraded readings and nuisance trips do not.
